name: GitHub Platform
description: Protects against destructive GitHub CLI operations like deleting repositories, gists, releases, or SSH keys.

destructive_patterns.name: gh-repo-delete
destructive_patterns.description: gh repo delete permanently deletes a GitHub repository. This cannot be undone.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a repository removes its code, issues, pull requests, releases, \ wiki, and Actions history together. GitHub can restore a deleted repository \ only within 90 days, only if the name has not been reused, and only via \ support — it is not a self-service undo.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - gh repo archive: makes it read-only while keeping everything visible \ (the engine gates this one too, but it is reversible) \ - gh repo edit --visibility private: hides it without destroying it

destructive_patterns.name: gh-repo-archive
destructive_patterns.description: gh repo archive makes a repository read-only. While reversible, it stops all write access.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Archiving is reversible, but until it is reversed nobody can push, open \ issues, or comment, and automation that writes to the repository starts \ failing. Unarchive from the web UI (Settings) or with the REST API.

\ Reverse it with: \ gh api -X PATCH repos/<owner>/<repo> -F archived=false

destructive_patterns.name: gh-gist-delete
destructive_patterns.description: gh gist delete permanently deletes a Gist.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Gist deletion is immediate and permanent — there is no trash and no \ support-side restore. Any URL you have shared, and anything embedding the \ Gist, breaks at once.

\ Save the contents first: \ gh gist view <id> > backup.txt

destructive_patterns.name: gh-release-delete
destructive_patterns.description: gh release delete permanently deletes a release.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a release destroys its uploaded assets. Anyone installing by that \ release URL — install scripts, CI pipelines, package managers pinned to it — \ starts getting 404s immediately, and the binaries cannot be recovered unless \ you still have them locally.

\ Safer alternative: \ - gh release edit <tag> --draft: unpublish while keeping the assets

destructive_patterns.name: gh-issue-delete
destructive_patterns.description: gh issue delete permanently deletes an issue.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Issue deletion is permanent and takes the whole discussion thread with it. \ Almost every reason to delete an issue is better served by closing it, which \ preserves the history and the cross-references other issues rely on.

\ Safer alternative: \ - gh issue close <number> --reason 'not planned'

destructive_patterns.name: gh-ssh-key-delete
destructive_patterns.description: gh ssh-key delete removes an SSH key, potentially breaking access.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Removing an SSH key takes effect immediately for every machine using it. If \ it is the key for the session you are in, or the only key on a remote host, \ you lose git push/pull access and may lock yourself out of automation that \ authenticates with it.

\ Confirm which key you are about to remove: \ gh ssh-key list

destructive_patterns.name: gh-secret-delete
destructive_patterns.description: gh secret delete removes GitHub Actions secrets.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Secret values are write-only — GitHub will not show you the value, so a \ deleted secret cannot be restored unless you hold it somewhere else. Every \ workflow referencing it starts failing on the next run, often mid-deploy.

\ Safer alternative: \ - gh secret set <NAME>: rotate the value in place, no window with it missing

destructive_patterns.name: gh-variable-delete
destructive_patterns.description: gh variable delete removes GitHub Actions variables.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Workflows referencing the variable resolve it to an empty string rather than \ failing loudly, so the breakage can be silent — a deploy target or feature \ flag quietly becomes blank.

\ Safer alternative: \ - gh variable set <NAME>: change the value without a window where it is unset

destructive_patterns.name: gh-repo-deploy-key-delete
destructive_patterns.description: gh repo deploy-key delete removes a deploy key and can break access.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deploy keys are how servers and CI clone this repository without a user \ account. Removing one breaks those consumers immediately, and the failure \ usually surfaces on someone else's next deploy rather than here.

\ Confirm what depends on it: \ gh repo deploy-key list

destructive_patterns.name: gh-run-cancel
destructive_patterns.description: gh run cancel stops a workflow run and may interrupt deployments.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Cancelling mid-run can leave a deployment half-applied: a job that has \ already pushed some resources stops before its cleanup or rollback steps. \ Check what the run is doing before stopping it.

\ Inspect first: \ gh run view <run-id>

destructive_patterns.name: gh-api-delete-actions-secret
destructive_patterns.description: gh api DELETE actions/secrets removes GitHub Actions secrets.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Secret values are write-only, so a deleted secret cannot be read back or \ restored. Every workflow referencing it fails on the next run.

\ Safer alternative: \ - gh secret set <NAME>: rotate the value in place via the first-class verb

destructive_patterns.name: gh-api-delete-actions-variable
destructive_patterns.description: gh api DELETE actions/variables removes GitHub Actions variables.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Workflows referencing a missing variable resolve it to an empty string rather \ than failing loudly, so the breakage is easy to miss.

\ Safer alternative: \ - gh variable set <NAME>: update the value via the first-class verb

destructive_patterns.name: gh-api-delete-hook
destructive_patterns.description: gh api DELETE hooks removes repository webhooks.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Removing a webhook silently stops every downstream integration it feeds — CI \ triggers, chat notifications, deployment hooks. Nothing errors; events simply \ stop arriving, so the failure surfaces late and somewhere else.

\ Inspect first, and note the config so it can be recreated: \ gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/hooks

destructive_patterns.name: gh-api-delete-deploy-key
destructive_patterns.description: gh api DELETE keys removes deploy keys.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deploy keys are how servers and CI clone this repository without a user \ account. Removing one breaks those consumers immediately, usually surfacing \ on someone else's next deploy.

\ Confirm what depends on it: \ gh repo deploy-key list

destructive_patterns.name: gh-api-delete-release
destructive_patterns.description: gh api DELETE releases removes GitHub releases.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a release destroys its uploaded assets. Install scripts and pinned \ CI jobs that fetch by that release URL start getting 404s immediately.

\ Safer alternative: \ - gh release edit <tag> --draft: unpublish while keeping the assets

destructive_patterns.name: gh-api-delete-repo
destructive_patterns.description: gh api DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo} permanently deletes a GitHub repository. This cannot be undone.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
This is the raw-API spelling of `gh repo delete`. It removes the code, \ issues, pull requests, releases, wiki, and Actions history together. GitHub \ can restore a deleted repository only within 90 days, only if the name has \ not been reused, and only via support.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - gh api -X PATCH repos/<owner>/<repo> -F archived=true: read-only, via the API \ - gh repo archive: the same thing via the first-class verb (the engine gates \ that one too, but archiving is reversible)

destructive_patterns.name: gh-api-delete-generic
destructive_patterns.description: gh api DELETE calls can be destructive. Please verify the endpoint.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
This is the catch-all for raw-API deletions whose endpoint this pack does not \ recognize, so the blast radius is unknown rather than known-large — it covers \ both `DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}` scale operations and routine ones like \ removing a label or an assignee.

\ Before reaching for a raw API DELETE, check whether `gh` has a first-class \ verb for it: those are more readable, and several are allowed outright. For \ example, sub-issue hierarchy has dedicated verbs: \ - gh issue edit <child> --remove-parent \ - gh issue edit <parent> --remove-sub-issue <number>

\ Preview what the endpoint returns before deleting it: \ gh api <endpoint>
